posts.title: Even parasites have parasites: Fungus infects powdery mildew
posts.excerpt: In the fungal kingdom, no one is safe from parasites—not even other parasites. By screening museum samples of powdery mildews up to about 150 years old, researchers discovered that not only is Ampelomyces quite common, but many specimens labeled as Ampelomyces are misidentified.

posts.title: Fluorescent probes reveal fluid-like barriers inside nuclear pores of living human cells
posts.excerpt: Our genetic material is hidden inside the nucleus of our cells, well protected by a double membrane. All molecules wishing to pass through must thread their way through one of several thousand nuclear pores. The scaffold structure of these pores is well known. However, exactly how transport takes place within them has been the subject of much debate. Researchers at Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz (JGU), the Max Planck Institute for Biophysics (MPI-BP) in Frankfurt am Main and Wuhan University in China have now shed light on the matter.

posts.title: Superconducting vortices provide experimental evidence that clogging is a phase transition
posts.excerpt: Clogging is a phenomenon in which moving particles get stuck, slowing or blocking the flow, but how this transition occurs has remained experimentally unproven. Researchers from Science Tokyo studied superconducting vortices to demonstrate that clogging is a nonequilibrium phase transition. Using a two-step measurement protocol, they distinguished clogging from conventional pinning and revealed that both transitions share a critical point, offering new insights into predicting and controlling clogging across diverse systems.

posts.excerpt: A new study quantifies, for the first time, the interrelationships and competing objectives of two major areas of action for reducing greenhouse gas emissions: the phaseout of fossil fuels and measures taken on natural land, such as farmland, forests and wetlands. It demonstrates how a well-balanced policy mix can keep costs low for both people and nature. The study, conducted at the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research (PIK), was published in Nature Sustainability.

posts.title: Bundesbüdchen in Bonn, Germany
posts.excerpt: In 1949, West Germany was debating the location for its provisional government. After lengthy back-and-forth—the mayor of Frankfurt, Walter Kolb, had even pre-recorded a victory speech—the choice came to Bonn. A university town known as little more than the birthplace of Beethoven, Bonn had seen little wartime damage, had few ties to the Third Reich, and lacked the gravitas that a larger city might have commanded to keep the government upon reunification. Yet while Bonn offered the fledgling Federal Republic a fresh start, it lacked the culinary infrastructure to satiate hungry politicians.

posts.title: Accidental discovery enables room-temperature recrystallization of molybdenum
posts.excerpt: Researchers at the University of Rochester and Technion–Israel Institute of Technology accidentally discovered a new way to rearrange the internal structure of molybdenum—an extremely heat-resistant metal—at room temperature. Molybdenum is typically used to reinforce nuclear reactors, jet engine turbine blades and rocket nozzles because it doesn't melt until it is heated to more than 2,600°C (4,712°F). Controlling its atomic structure at room temperature could open the door to more applications, including next-generation semiconductors.

posts.title: Not a 'night owl' yet: Extraordinary bird fossil from Messel Pit suggests species still hunted by day
posts.excerpt: An exceptionally well-preserved, approximately 47-million-year-old owl fossil from the UNESCO World Heritage Site Messel provides new clues as to when owls became nocturnal. posts.title: Smart use of trees and crops brings best yield
posts.excerpt: Cultivating crops—such as wheat, barley and rye—alongside rows of trees is a system of agroforestry that is known as "alley-cropping." It serves many functions: in addition to enhancing ecosystems and biodiversity, it can also counteract the negative effects of growing crops in treeless open land. The advantages of alley-cropping come from the interaction between trees and crops, resulting in improved soil quality, reduced wind erosion, enhanced nutrient cycling, and climate change mitigation through increased carbon capture.

posts.title: Thunderstruck: what does the future hold for lightning?
posts.excerpt: Humans have always been awed by the power and beauty of lightning. How does the experience and understanding of it change in a warming world? posts.title: A carefully timed pair of light pulses can amplify the motion of atomic layers in a quantum material
posts.excerpt: The principle "Work smarter, not harder!" apparently also applies to controlling quantum materials with light. posts.title: Molecular imaging reveals how shape-shifting protein complex captures DNA and holds separate sections together
posts.excerpt: Researchers at Kanazawa University and the National Institute of Genetics in Japan have used high-speed atomic force microscopy to observe how a group of proteins known as Smc5/6 interacts with DNA. The images reveal how this structure opens and closes, captures DNA and brings separate sections together. The researchers also observed Smc5/6 holding twisted sections of DNA in place, producing more tightly packed arrangements. The findings, published in Nature Communications,  provide new insights into the molecular processes that contribute to the maintenance and repair of genetic material.
